answer: Yes, use the export command: 'export [<variable>=[<value>]]'. Variables are referenced as ${variable} in any CLI command, which is especially useful in CLI scripts. The variable name can be any alphanumeric name; the value can be any supported character, including spaces. They do NOT survive logout: variables are locally defined per session and are removed after the session is closed. 'export SLOT_NUMBER=2' declares one, 'export SLOT_NUMBER=' deletes it, and bare 'export' lists all existing variables (output looks like export MYSESSIONID="10.100.152.29:56154" / export MYUSERNAME="admin"). Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Both launch a Linux bash shell from the CLI and are Operational Mode only, and both accept a single command to execute instead of an interactive session; exit returns you to the CLI prompt. 'shell [-h] [shell command]' runs on the node itself, launched as the currently logged in user with that user's command access; access can be limited to users in the NA, NE and TT user-groups, and certain commands can be run with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo' (permitted list includes /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and a set of /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts). 'gshell [-h] [<cmd>]' instead launches the bash shell inside a Guest Container, and has a pre-condition: the dial-out server must be configured for the command to execute properly. Example: gshell ls -l.

No. 'kill-session <session-id>' closes any established session independently of its type (CLI, NETCONF, etc), but the <session-id> must match an existing session and cannot match the id of your current session; to end your own session use the normal 'exit' command instead. The session-id is a string in the form '<ip-address>:<port>'. Use 'show session' first to display the list of current sessions and pick the id. Access mode: Operational mode. Example: kill-session 10.24.11.25:56212.

Use the message command: 'message [message-content=]<value> [[target=]<value>]'. By default the message is broadcast to all CLI sessions (target default = all), so 'message "System will reboot in 5 minutes"' reaches everyone. message content is a string of 1-4096 characters. The target values are: all (all CLI sessions), local (only local sessions: serial console or CRAFT), remote (only remote sessions, e.g. SSH), session-id (only one specific session), and username (all CLI sessions of a specific user). Example targeted form: message "System reboot in 5 minutes" 0.0.0.0:36. Access mode: Operational mode. The command can also be executed from NETCONF and RESTCONF, but the message is only sent to CLI sessions.

Properties are type-specific, auto instantiated by the system but user configurable, addressed as property-<card-name>/<property-name>. Syntax: 'set property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value <value>]' and 'show property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value] [description]'. Two property-names are supported: fast-client-recovery, which indicates whether fast client signal recovery is enabled or disabled in case of client signal failures (values disabled, enabled; default disabled); and max-packet-length, the maximum packet length supported by the CHM6 / CHM6L DCO (range 1518 to 18000; default 1518). Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: set property-1-5/fast-client-recovery value enabled.

Use run. Syntax: 'run task [[task-name=]<value>]' and 'run script [-q] [-y] [-e=<value>] [-r] [[script-name=]<value>] [[arguments=]<value>]'. Pre-condition: the task or the script to be called must already be defined. task-name is a leafref to /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:scheduled-tasks/ioa-ne:task/ioa-ne:name; script-name is a relative path to the script directory, with optional arguments as a string. Flags: -q runs the script in quiet mode (only command output shown, otherwise both the command and its output are shown), -r executes the script as a declarative config script, replacing system configuration with the script content, and -e sets the error option: continue (default), stop or rollback. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. Examples: run task collect-diag; run script config.cli -e=stop -q.

Both add/set/show/delete user-configurable scheduled commands in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and both share enabled (true/false, default true), command (string), command-type (CLI command), frequency, start-time, end-time and persistent (true/false, default true, meaning the task survives a system restart). 'task-<name>' is the fuller object: name is a string 0..64 characters, command is 1..1024 characters, and it adds label, alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and number-of-runs (no-limit or 1..65535, default no-limit, applicable when frequency is configured); its read-only show attributes are task-status (scheduled, disabled, finished, ongoing; default scheduled), next-run, previous-run, previous-result (success or fail) and previous-output. 'scheduled-task-<name>' uses the same fields but exposes them via add/set with coarser values (task-status true/false default false, previous-result 1 or 2) and is listed with 'show scheduled-tasks'.

Only if you are an SA user. 'show session-<session-id> [session-user] [session-type] [session-protocol] [created-time] [local-ip-address] [dial-out-server-name]' shows the currently established management layer sessions, but only SA users can access the list of all sessions; remaining users can only see their own session. session-id is the IP address and transport port of the session, or 'NA' if the session is initiated from the serial port. session-type values: cli, snmp, netconf, restconf, webgui, gnmi. session-protocol values: telnet, telnet-raw, serial, ssh, ssh-raw, https, http. RESTCONF sessions are visible in CLI when Cookie Based Authentication is used; that session has a keep-alive of 5 minutes by default, changeable with the restconf cookie-timeout attribute. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. 'set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...]' takes at least one attribute-value pair, all belonging to the same managed entity; if no entity id is given the currently scoped entity is used. Wildcards (*) set an attribute on multiple instances at once: as replacement of the whole instance key (card-*), of a single instance key (port-1-4-*, port-1-*-3), of all following keys to the right (odu-1-4,5,6,7-*), for auto-completing instance keys (user-admin*, ethernet-*) and for auto-completing attribute names (admin* instead of admin-state). You can also use [] for ranges (card-1-[1..4]) or lists (interface-[DCN,CRAFT]), and filters of the form <attribute>=<value>, e.g. 'set port port-type=line admin-state lock'. The command asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances; -f forces without confirmation and -v only validates. Example: set port-1-4* admin-state lock.

User access to the shell command can be limited to users in the NA, NE and TT user-groups. 'shell [-h] [shell command]' is Operational Mode only and launches the Linux bash shell as the currently logged in user, allowing only the commands accessible to that user; exit the shell the usual way (for example the 'exit' command) to return to the CLI prompt. A single shell command can also be run inline, e.g. shell ifconfig, shell vi, shell editor. Certain commands/scripts can be launched with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo'; the permitted set includes /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and a list of /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts (download.sh, install_os.sh, config_ip.sh, docker.sh, CopyLogsToUSB.sh and others). Use single quotes for composed commands: shell 'sudo netstat -alnp | grep sshd'.

Yes. If a user executes a show command which generates more than 50000 objects, an error message is displayed to indicate that the output is too large. Narrow the request instead: give a specific <entity-id> or <entity-type>, add filters of the form <attribute>=<value>, or use wildcards (card-*, port-1-4-*, admin* for admin-state) and ranges/lists (card-1-[1..4], interface-[DCN,CRAFT]). Limit recursion with -r=<n>, which operates the command recursively for n levels down (full recursion if n is not provided). Other useful flags are -c (container instances only), -a (attributes only), -x (configuration/read-write attributes only), -o (state/read-only only), -t (tabular), -l (long) and -d (show default values). Piping through '| more' displays long output page by page.

Yes for alarms and card insertion. 'simulate [trigger=]<value> ([holder-AID=]<value> [type=]<value> [[subtype=]<value>] | [alarmed-entity=]<value> [alarm-type=]<value> [[alarm-direction=]<value>] [[alarm-location=]<value>])'. Trigger values: raise-alarm, clear-alarm, plug-in-fru, plug-out-fru, but note that plug-out-fru is not supported. Equipment simulation needs the holder-AID (string 1..64) matching the card slot or the tom port, plus the card type; subtype is optional. Alarm simulation needs alarmed-entity and alarm-type; if either is omitted when clearing, all simulated alarms are cleared. alarm-direction and alarm-location both default to auto (selected automatically by the system). The command works in a simulator and on a real system, but on a real system simulation cannot be done if it interferes with real HW, for example you cannot simulate plugout of hardware that is physically present. Access mode: Operational mode. Example: simulate plug-in-fru 1-5.

Yes. 'sleep <time in seconds>' specifies a delay, and the sleep time may be an arbitrary floating point number, so fractions of a second are allowed. 'sleep 1' waits one second and 'sleep 0.1' waits 100 milliseconds. The only flag is -h, which displays help for the command. Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, so it can be used inside CLI scripts run with 'run script'.

Add a task with no frequency: a task with no frequency interval configured is a single-occurrence task (in scheduled-task the guide states that an empty frequency, the default, represents a single-occurrence task). Syntax: 'add task-<name> command <value> [enabled <value>] [label <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [command-type <value>] [frequency <value>] [number-of-runs <value>] [start-time <value>] [end-time <value>] [persistent <value>]'. start-time is the timestamp to start the task. The guide's own example is: add task-db_backup_once command "upload database file-server=xfr1" start-time 2021-04-23T05:05:00+00:00 alarm-report-control allowed label "DB Backup once". Note: this requires that the file server xfr1 be configured before the command is used. Defaults: enabled true, persistent true (survives a system restart), command-type cli, alarm-report-control allowed, end-time never. Check progress with 'show task-<name>' fields task-status (scheduled/disabled/finished/ongoing), next-run, previous-run, previous-result (success/fail) and previous-output.

'terminate' stops a running operation, Operational Mode. Forms: 'terminate location-led <entity>' stops a location led test previously started with activate on a chassis or a card (no effect if no test is active); 'terminate otdr [entity=]<value>' stops an ongoing OTDR measurement for the given port; 'terminate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<value>' stops a manually triggered OTDR based Raman fiber check on an OTS-R entity, aborting the scan abruptly, restoring otdr ne function attributes and reverting ots-r-auto-otdr auto-otdr-state (if that state was fail, the PUMPS-DISABLED-OTDR-TEST-FAILED alarm is raised again); 'terminate loopback [entity=]<value>[,<value>]*' terminates WSS loopback on NMC entities, and all channels under the loopback in a degree must be terminated; 'terminate cable-id' stops CableID verification. Confirmation for CableID: the test is known to be terminated once cable-id-status cable-id-state changes to idle, checked with 'show cable-id cable-id-status'. Termination is per port-pair, so the maximum delay is one port-pair verification time.

'update [type=]<value> [[entity-id=]<value>[,<value>]*]' triggers a specific predefined update action on an object attribute rather than assigning an arbitrary value the way set does, and it is Operational mode only (set works in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). The type values are: span-loss-alarm-threshold, which updates/re-evaluates the OTS attribute span-loss-alarm-threshold; filter-insertion-date-now, which updates the chassis dust filter insertion date to the current date; set-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to under commissioning state; and clear-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to Ready for Service state. The last two apply to NE entities in SLTE systems. Multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*). Examples: update span-loss-alarm-threshold ots-1-1-dwdm-line; update filter-insertion-date-now chassis.

Use the auxiliary commands tic and toc. tic starts a timer for the typed command, and toc displays the elapsed time since the timer was started and the command was executed by the system. Both are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Wrap a single command as 'tic;show log;toc'. For a list of commands (a script) put them on separate lines between the two, for example: tic / ;show log / ;traceroute 10.128.1.1 / ;toc. These are add-on auxiliary commands intended for evaluating the system response to a command or script.

Yes. Use 'help -s <keyword> [<keyword> ...]'. It searches the provided keyword(s) in all commands help text and displays the matches in order of relevance. Partial keywords can be provided using a wild card, for example 'help -s inventory' or 'help -s data*'. The rest of the help system: '?' on its own displays the list of all available commands; 'help <command/container/attribute>' (e.g. help show) explains how the command, container or attribute can be used; '<command> ?' (show ?) lists the possible addressable parameters; '<command> -?' (show -?) lists the possible options; '<command> -h' (show -h) shows the complete help; '<command> <container> ?' shows the container's hierarchy sub-containers and attribute list; '<command> <attribute> ?' lists the attributes of the given container.

Yes to both: aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions, so an alias survives your logout and other operators see it. 'alias [<name>=<value>]' defines a more user-friendly alphanumeric string for one or more commands, a container, an attribute or values; 'alias' with no arguments prints the current list of aliases in the form 'name=value'. Quotes must be used for multi-word values, e.g. alias sa='show alarm'; a single word alias is alias s=show. Aliases can reference other aliases, and the <name> of an alias can be used without resolving it by putting it in quotes. Remove them with the unalias command. Access mode: Operational mode.

'unalias -a' removes all defined aliases. Syntax: 'unalias -h', 'unalias -a', 'unalias [<name> ...]', so you can also remove specific ones (unalias foo, or unalias bar baz qux). Removing an alias has impact on all sessions and users, because aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions, so clearing them affects every operator on the node, not just you. The command is always successful unless a supplied <name> is not a defined alias. Aliases can be added and visualized again with the 'alias' command. Access mode: Operational Mode.

'tree [-a|-o|-d=depth] ([<entity id> ...])' controls this. Use -d=depth to set the maximum display depth, i.e. the number of levels to be displayed; if not specified, all levels are displayed by default, e.g. 'tree -d=2'. Use -a to display entity ancestors only, showing just the target entity along with all its ancestors, e.g. 'tree -a interface-DCN' or 'tree -a port usb'. -o displays a tree based on a YANG top node. The base of the tree is the current working entity or the provided entity id, e.g. 'tree card-1-1'. Only managed entities are shown, including all existing instances, with no attribute names or values, and output uses the UTF-8 character set. You can also page it with 'tree | more'. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

All three change the currently selected managed entity and the effect is visible on the CLI path banner; all are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. 'edit [-h] <entity-id> [<entity-id> ...]' navigates to any entity in the hierarchy; the entity IDs can be absolute (starting from the root of the system) or relative to the current entity shown in the path banner, and the attempt to edit a nonexistent entity instance will fail. Examples: edit port-1-5-T1, edit card-1-1, or relative edit chassis-1 slot-2. 'up [-h]' brings the current path up by one path level, to the parent, and supports no parameters; at the hierarchy top level it has no impact. 'top [-h]' brings the current path straight to the top of the managed entity hierarchy, [ne].

Use the history command. 'history [-h]' displays the current session's command history as a numbered list. Each command can be repeated using '!<n>', where n is the number in the history list, and '!!' repeats the previous command. To find a particular entry, filter the listing with piped commands, for example: history | include 'show'. Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The list covers the current session only.

Nothing happens: at the hierarchy top level the 'up' command has no impact. 'up [-h]' brings the current path up by one path level in the managed entity hierarchy, changing the currently selected managed entity to its parent level, and the effect is visible on the CLI banner; the command does not support any parameters. So from [card-1-5], up goes to [equipment], and up again goes to [ne]; issuing up again at [ne] leaves you at [ne]. Related commands: 'edit' navigates to any entity in the hierarchy, 'top' navigates to the top of the hierarchy root. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

They do the same job, and the guide states each is the same as the other: both are piped commands (<command> | grep <filter> / <command> | include <filter>) that only display lines matching <filter>, do a case insensitive comparison (show | grep abc is equivalent to show | grep ABC), accept multiple words separated by spaces when enclosed in quotes, support regex, and can be chained with other piped commands. The difference is that grep has several additional filtering options: -a=<n> (number of lines of context to show after the actual match), -b=<n> (number of lines of context to show before the actual match) and -n (displays line numbers in the result). include takes only <filter> and -h. Related filters: exclude removes matching lines, begin starts output at a matching line, until ends output at a matching line.
